Dear all

I've found out, that the files causing the erros had quite a few lines with "0,0,0\n" values to start with.

I've solved the issue manually with a Python script that removes these lines, corrects the "Start Time" in the header and writes the output to a new .csv file that can be processed by GGIR.

What I don't understand is, why GGIR doesn't deal with that automatically? Sadly, my R skills are not up to the task to really troubleshoot it in depth.

Here is the code if someone wants to use it. I've run it with Python 3.10.8.

Best regards
Christian

The code:
#!/usr/bin/env python
# coding: utf-8

from pathlib import Path
import time

def evaluate_start_of_data(file):
    """This function takes as input a Path object or a pathstring of a Actigraphy.csv file"""
    file = Path(file)
    with open(file, "r") as f:
        lines = f.readlines()
        head = lines[0:11]  # please make sure that your header has the same format

        number_of_zero_lines = 0
        for line in lines[11:]:
            if line == '0,0,0\n' or line == '"0","0","0"\n':
                number_of_zero_lines += 1
            else:
                break
        endindex_of_zero_lines = number_of_zero_lines + 11  # number of "0,0,0\n" lines + length of header
        body = lines[endindex_of_zero_lines:]
        return head, body, number_of_zero_lines

def calculate_offset(sample_frequency, number_of_zero_lines):
    """Calculate the seconds with only '0,0,0\n'"""
    seconds_of_zero_lines = number_of_zero_lines / sample_frequency
    return seconds_of_zero_lines

def repair_file(file, sample_frequency=30):
    """find head, number_of_zero_lines and body of actigraphy"""
    head, body, number_of_zero_lines = evaluate_start_of_data(file)

    offset = calculate_offset(sample_frequency, number_of_zero_lines)

    # replace the "Start Time 00:00:00\n" string with the to be removed time interval
    corrected_start_time = "Start Time " + time.strftime("%H:%M:%S", time.gmtime(offset)) + "\n"
    head[2] = corrected_start_time  # make sure that this corresponds to the correct line in your file
    print(f"Removed {offset} seconds of empty data from {file.name <http://file.name>}.\n{corrected_start_time}")

    # write to a new outputfile
    outputfile = file.stem + "_zeroes_removed.csv"
    outputpath = file.parent / outputfile
    with open(outputpath, "w") as output:
        output.writelines(head)
        output.writelines(body)

def repair_all_files_in_directory(directory_path, sample_frequency=30):
    """Apply the repair_file function to all files in a directory"""
    directory_path = Path(directory_path)
    for file in directory_path.iterdir():
        repair_file(file)

messages.body_plain:
Hi John,

The script looks good to me.

I have never used the Galland algorithm before in my research, but this is how it is used in GGIR. If you are using hip-worn accelerometers, consider using the "HorAngle" algorithm to define de sleep period time windows (sensor.location = "hip", HASPT.algo = "HorAngle", longitudinal_axis = 2, the longitudinal axis should be the one aligned with the spine [vertical axis], which in most brands I have seen it is the second column in the raw data, but it would be good if you double-check this in your data).

The cut-points look good, I see you are using the Evenson cut-points as provided in the manuscript, and you are using the same epoch length they used in the calibration study. Very minor point is that the calibration study reported a threshold.lig of 26, not 25, but I can't see this having a strong effect in your analyses.

Hope this helps.

Best,
Jairo

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] part 5 missing day
messages.body_plain:
Hi Leaf,

Thanks for your clear message with detailed description and link to your output.

GGIR Part 2 attempts to report all days that meet the number of valid hours specified by argument includedaycrit.

GGIR Part 4 only attempts to detect sleep for noon-noon windows that have the midnight timestamp and the number of valid hours for that window meets the criteria specified by includenightcrit. So if you recording starts at midnight GGIR will count it as a night (night 1) but not analyse it as there are less than 16 hours in the night.

GGIR Part 5 only shows days where the day starts and ends with estimate sleep. The only exception is that if the recording starts at or before midnight and sleep estimates are missing, it will still attempt to classify the wake-up time for the first day. Part 5 is only meaningful when days have sufficient valid data. So, please not try to tweak GGIR only to get extra rows in part 5 output as the values will be rubbish because they no longer reflect a complete day and for time-use analyses in particular this will introduce a bias in your analyses.

Never use argument "recordingEndSleepHour" unless you have good reason to assume that all your participants were asleep before that time as clarified in the documentation. As this is not realistic for adults this should ideally only be used for young children and even then with extreme caution.

As a side note - A lot of studies seem to have been collecting 7 days of data without realising that 7 days of data is insufficient to derive 7 days of 24 hour behaviour estimates. To do that we would ideally need at least 9 days of data, because then we have 8 complete nights and 7 complete days in between those nights. This is not a limitation of GGIR but a challenge that would apply to any software that aims to provide robust 24/7 estimates of behaviour.

Best wishes,

Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dr van Hees and fellow GGIRers,

Hoping someone can help here.  I have used GeneActiv watches and GGIR to process my data.  My watches were all set to start recording at my local time which is timezone of Australia/Melbourne, usually start recording at 00:00hour.

1. Timezone issue: Out of 65 participants, I had 13 files which had time stamp errors.

In GGIR csv file, the recording timestamps are correct, e.g., start recording at

2021-11-17 00:00:00:500.
In GGIR csv file, I notice the start time is set wrongly to: Start Time 2010-09-16 09:10:00:000
When data was processed in GGIR using the BIN files only, I get the following output.  The date and time are wrong as they reflect the start time as per CSV file instead of when the movement recording start. See image 1 below titled "Wrong tz".

I had previously been able to use desiredtz=”USA/ Hawaii” in GGIR (version 2.6.0, ran on Windows) to change the output to this, which appears correct according to my record.  See image below titled "Corrected by desiredtz".

However, I tried to rerun the same file using the same desiredtz = “America/Hawaii” in GGIR (version 2.9.0, on Mac), I received an output where the timezone error was not corrected and it was as if the desiredtz code had no effect.  I ran my files with and without the timezone correction and both times it gave me the same results. I am wondering if there a specific way to ensure desiredtz is used in version 2.9.0?

2. Guider = Sleeplog with no sleep log provided.  When I went back to rerun the same analysis in PC using version 2.6.0, but this time without sleep log, the output in Part 4 stated Guider = Sleeplog instead of HDCZA.

Please advise how I can get desiredtz to work in GGIR version 2.9.0 and how to ensure the default HDCZA algothrim is used.

I attach my GGIR script below for your reference.

g.shell.GGIR(

  mode=c(1,2,3,4,5),

  datadir="C:/Input_Files",

  outputdir="C:/Output_Files",

  do.report=c(2,4,5),

  desiredtz=”USA/ Hawaii”,

  #=====================

  # Part 2

  #=====================

  strategy = 1,

  hrs.del.start = 0,          hrs.del.end = 0,

  maxdur = 18,                 includedaycrit = 16,

  qwindow=c(0,24),

  mvpathreshold =c(100),

  bout.metric = 4,

  excludefirstlast = FALSE,

  includenightcrit = 16,

  overwrite = TRUE,

  #=====================

  # Part 3 + 4

  #=====================

  def.noc.sleep = 1,

  outliers.only = TRUE,

  criterror = 4,

  do.visual = TRUE,

  #=====================

  # Part 5

  #=====================

  threshold.lig = 30, threshold.mod = 100,  threshold.vig = 400,

  boutcriter = 0.8,      boutcriter.in <http://boutcriter.in> = 0.9,     boutcriter.lig = 0.8,

  boutcriter.mvpa = 0.8, boutdur.in <http://boutdur.in> = c(1,10,30), boutdur.lig = c(1,10),

  boutdur.mvpa = c(1),

  includedaycrit.part5 = 2/3,

  #=====================

  # Visual report

  #=====================

  timewindow = c("WW"),

  visualreport=TRUE)

Thank you, all!

Cheers,

Susie

As of very recently the beta version of GGIR on GitHub (release 2.9-2) does facilitate this, but it has only been tested so far on data collected in The Netherlands. As a result, it would be good to have people test it in different date format en language zones of the world.

As you will see the key argument is dataFormat. Additionally you need to make sure the first value of argument windowsizes aligns with the epoch size in seconds of the data. GGIR tries to extract this from the data but to be 100% sure we also expect you specify it as input argument.

To install this version of GGIR do:

install.packages("remotes')
remotes::install_github("wadpac/GGIR", ref = "2.9-2")

If you have problems please report back and sent me an example file to look at.

Sorry for the delay in getting back to you. You are correct, you still need an algorithm to identify the sleep period time, for example the HorAngle algorithm. Your script looks fine to me. I am not aware of any study that has used the HorAngle yet.

As for the metrics, yes, setting acc.metric = ENMO and the Galland algorithm would provide physical activity using ENMO and sleep using counts.

Note also that the Galland's algorithm was developed in infants with accelerometers placed on the shin, not on the hip, just wanted to point this out as you are using hip data.

Best,
Jairo

messages.subject_clean: Time not correct in summary files
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Thanks for creating such a great resource!

I'm working on some day-segment analysis with .gt3x files and am finding the times are offset in the output, but not in the raw data or meta files:

The data was initialized/collected and analyzed in CST (Canada), however the output in the summary files appears to be offset by +11 hours. In this case, the recording should run 0730-1300, but instead the output has times starting at 1830 and running into the next day (i.e. apparent when running 1-hr windows via qwindow). This also means the times in any activity log do not align (unless they are also offset by the 11 hours).

The timestamps in the meta files appear to be correct, as well as in basic plots of epoched enmo in the meta files and the raw gt3x read into R (read.gt3x).

I've tried various changes to desiredtz and configtz, but they most often have no effect.

I'm using Rstudio (R 4.1.0) on Windows 10. Attached is a sample meta file and long format summary file with the offset (generated from 1-hr windows via qwindow). Here's a sample GT3X file: https://www.dropbox.com/s/6mw0idwwigtckq0/sample.gt3x?dl=0

Any suggestions?

Thanks in advance,
Rob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent,

I found the IDs are not used correctly in part4 sleep reports, for example,

EVISX3          ELP29O__034637_2017-12-01 09-09-28.bin.RData   EVISX3    sleeplog

 The ID was ELP29O in the old GGIR version. Please kindly advise me if I could still use GGIR2.9.0 outputs. Hope you never merge the data using ID and use filename as the only link to do the data merge.

By the way,  I found out that GGIR use the later sleep period since this data includes two separate 14 days observation in 2017 and 2019, but part2 activity data use the earlier period in 2017. This leads to no overlap in part2 and part4.  In GGIR2.2, I do not have this issue since both parts use the earlier period in 2017.

Please kindly advise. I have sent this sample by email yesterday.

Thank you so much.
Best,
Wei
